lines.text: I left Earth two years ago. I just landed. And everyone I knew has been gone for a *hundred years.*
This isn't science fiction. It's how time really works. And it's the real problem with traveling to the stars.
Time doesn't tick the same for everyone. The faster you move through space, the slower you move through *time.*
Picture the simplest clock possible. A flash of light, bouncing between two mirrors. Every bounce is one tick.
Put that clock on a spaceship. On board, the light goes straight up and down. Same as always.
But watch from Earth. The ship is moving, so the light has to travel on a slant to reach the other mirror. A *longer path.*
And light has a speed limit. About 300,000 kilometers per second. The same for everyone, always.
A longer path at the same speed takes longer. So from Earth, the ship's clock ticks *slower.*
Everything on board slows with it. Your watch. Your heartbeat. You. And you'd never feel it.
At normal speeds, it's tiny, but real. GPS satellites correct for it every day, or your map would drift about ten kilometers.
But close to light speed, it explodes. At 90 percent, your clock runs at less than half speed.
At 99 percent, one seventh. At 99.99 percent, *one seventieth.* One year for you. Seventy on Earth.
So let's take a trip. A star fifty light-years away, at 99.99 percent of light speed, there and back.
For you, the whole trip takes about a year and a half.
On Earth, a hundred years pass. Everyone you said goodbye to is *gone.*
And it's not just perspective. You're the one who turned around, so you're the one who's *younger.*
Go bigger. Accelerate at a comfortable one g the whole way, and you reach the Andromeda galaxy in about 28 years.
On Earth, two and a half million years go by. Humans might not even exist anymore.
That's the real problem with space travel. It's not getting there. It's that there's *no one to come back to.*
Unless you don't move through space at all. In 1994, physicist Miguel Alcubierre found a loophole in Einstein's equations.
Squeeze space in front of the ship, stretch it out behind. The ship sits still in a bubble, and space itself carries it. Like a moving walkway.
Since the ship isn't really moving through space, its clock doesn't slow down. You'd age right along with everyone at home.
You could actually *come home.*
The catch? It needs negative energy, which we don't know how to make, and may not exist in the amounts it would take.
And faster-than-light travel could, in theory, let you arrive before you left. Breaking cause and effect.
So for now, the stars are a one-way trip. Not in distance. In *time.*
If you could leave tonight, and come back in two million years... would you go?
